front: What are the two `stop_reason` values that control an agentic loop, and what does each mean?
back: `"tool_use"` — Claude wants to call a tool; execute it and continue the loop. `"end_turn"` — Claude is finished; stop the loop and show the result.

front: Name the three agentic-loop termination anti-patterns called out by the exam.
back: (1) Parsing assistant text for completion phrases. (2) Using an arbitrary iteration cap as the primary stop mechanism. (3) Checking for the presence of assistant text content as a completion signal.

front: Why must tool results be explicitly appended to conversation history between loop iterations?
back: Each API call is stateless — Claude has no memory between calls and only reasons over what's in the message history you send it.

front: In hub-and-spoke multi-agent orchestration, who handles all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and routing?
back: The coordinator. Subagents never communicate directly with each other — everything routes through the coordinator.

front: If every subagent executed its assigned subtask correctly but a report's topic coverage is too narrow, where's the root cause?
back: In the coordinator's task decomposition step — the subtask list itself was too narrow, not the subagents' execution.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.2; Exam Guide §9 Q7

front: What does an iterative refinement loop do when the coordinator detects a coverage gap in a synthesis draft?
back: It re-delegates to search/analysis with a targeted query aimed at the specific gap, then re-invokes synthesis — not a full pipeline restart.

front: What must a coordinator's `allowedTools` include for it to be able to spawn subagents at all?
back: `"Task"` — without it in allowedTools, the coordinator has no mechanism to invoke subagents, regardless of prompt wording.

front: In study-guide notation, what do the `AgentDefinition` fields `system_prompt` and `allowed_tools` configure? (Note: current SDK docs name these `prompt` and `tools`.)
back: `system_prompt` defines the subagent's role/behavior; `allowed_tools` restricts which tools it may call (principle of least privilege).
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.3; guide_en.md §3.2; verified against platform.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

front: Do subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history?
back: No. Subagents run with isolated context — all needed information must be explicitly included in the `Task` prompt.

front: How should a coordinator spawn several independent subagents to minimize latency?
back: Emit multiple `Task` tool calls within a single coordinator response so they execute in parallel, rather than one call per turn.

front: Give the canonical example of a programmatic prerequisite gate from the exam guide.
back: Block `process_refund` (and `lookup_order`) until `get_customer` has returned a verified customer ID.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.4; Exam Guide §9 Q1

front: What fields belong in a structured handoff summary when escalating to a human agent?
back: Customer ID, root cause, actions already taken, recommended action, and refund amount (if applicable) — the human has no access to the conversation transcript.

front: What does a `PostToolUse` hook do, and give an example use.
back: It intercepts a tool's result after execution, before the model sees it — used to normalize heterogeneous data (e.g., Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) into a consistent format.

front: What does a `PreToolUse` interception hook do, and give the exam's canonical example?
back: It fires before a tool call executes, letting you block or redirect it — e.g., block any `process_refund` call over $500 and redirect to human escalation.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.5; Exam Guide §9 Q1; verified against platform.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks

front: Hooks vs. prompt instructions: which gives a deterministic guarantee, and which gives probabilistic compliance?
back: Hooks run in code every time = deterministic guarantee. Prompt instructions = probabilistic compliance (the model usually, not always, complies).

front: When should you use prompt chaining (fixed pipeline) vs. dynamic adaptive decomposition?
back: Prompt chaining: task structure is predictable and repeats the same shape (e.g., a review template). Dynamic decomposition: full scope is unknown up front and each step depends on what's discovered.

front: What's the recommended two-pass structure for reviewing a large, multi-file pull request?
back: A per-file local-analysis pass for each changed file, plus a separate cross-file integration pass — this avoids attention dilution.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.6; Exam Guide §9 Q12; guide_en.md §8.3

front: What does `--resume <session-name>` do?
back: Continues a specific named prior conversation, bringing back its accumulated context (files read, findings, decisions).

front: What does `fork_session` do?
back: Creates an independent branch from a shared analysis baseline to explore a divergent approach — the original session is unaffected and both share context only up to the fork point.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.7; guide_en.md §5.10; verified against platform.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions

front: You resume a session after some of the files it investigated have changed. What should you do?
back: Explicitly tell the agent which specific files changed, so it does targeted re-analysis of just those — don't resume silently or require full re-exploration.

front: When is starting a fresh session with a structured summary more reliable than resuming?
back: When prior tool results are substantially stale (files changed a lot, or a long time has passed) — resuming would carry forward outdated tool output the agent might trust.
